'''Laura Faye Landweber''' is an American [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]]. {{As of|2016}}, she is a professor of [[biochemistry]] and [[molecular biophysics]] and of [[biological sciences]] at [[Columbia University]]. Previously, she was a professor of [[ecology]] and [[evolutionary biology]] at [[Princeton University]]. She specializes in RNA-mediated [[Epigenetics|epigenetic]] inheritance and [[molecular evolution]].

==Education==
Landweber graduated summa cum laude with an A.B. in molecular biology from [[Princeton University]] in 1989 after completing a 50-page-long senior thesis titled "A Method for Evolutionary [[Sequence analysis|Sequence Analysis]] of [[Gene]]s and [[Pseudogene]]s Using the [[Polymerase chain reaction|Polymerase Chain Reaction]]: Applications to the [[Mouse]] [[T-complex 1|Tcp-1 Gene]]" in which she described linear PCR.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Landweber|first=Laura Faye|editor-last=Princeton University. Department of Molecular Biology|title=A Method for Evolutionary Sequence Analysis of Genes and Pseudogenes Using the Polymerase Chain Reaction: Applications to the Mouse Tcp-1 Gene|year=1989 |url=http://arks.princeton.edu/ark:/88435/dsp01j9602255j|language=English}}</ref>

She received her M.A. and Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1991 and 1993, respectively. Her doctoral dissertation is titled "RNA editing and the evolution of mitochondrial DNA in kinetoplastid protozoa."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/~lfl/LandweberCV.pdf|title=Laura Landweber|last=|first=|date=19 January 2016|website=Princeton University|publisher=|access-date=12 November 2016}}</ref>

== Research career ==
In 1994, Landweber became a faculty member of Princeton University at the age of 26.

In a 2000 paper published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]'' on [[biocomputer]]s, Landweber solved chess's knights problem, where one determines how many non-attacking knights can be placed on a chessboard, using a test tube of RNA,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Hopkin|first1=Karen|title=The Fast Track to Success|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/24429/title/The-Fast-Track-to-Success/|work=The Scientist|date=November 1, 2006}}</ref> a breakthrough in [[DNA computing]].

Laura Landweber has also studied the evolution of the [[genetic code]]<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Knight |first1=Robin D |last2=Landweber |first2=Laura F |title=The Early Evolution of the Genetic Code |journal=Cell |date=June 2000 |volume=101 |issue=6 |pages=569–572 |doi=10.1016/S0092-8674(00)80866-1|pmid=10892641 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and the scrambled genomes of [[ciliate]]s such as [[Oxytricha]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Landweber |first1=LF |title=Genetics. Why genomes in pieces? |journal=Science |date=19 October 2007 |volume=318 |issue=5849 |pages=405–7 |doi=10.1126/science.1150280 |pmid=17947572|s2cid=86023076 }}</ref> Her laboratory has supported the notion that the code was no accident but arose from affinities between the nucleic acid [[codons]] and their cognate [[amino acid]]s.<ref name=":1" />  Her studies of the massive rearrangements of the [[genome]] in the [[micronucleus]] of Oxytricha showed an unsuspected role for [[non-coding RNA]] in directing the process [[Epigenetics|epigenetically.]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nowacki |first1=M |last2=Vijayan |first2=V |last3=Zhou |first3=Y |last4=Schotanus |first4=K |last5=Doak |first5=TG |last6=Landweber |first6=LF |title=RNA-mediated epigenetic programming of a genome-rearrangement pathway |journal=Nature |date=10 January 2008 |volume=451 |issue=7175 |pages=153–8 |doi=10.1038/nature06452 |pmid=18046331 |pmc=2647009|bibcode=2008Natur.451..153N }}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
*1999 – [[Sigma Xi]] Young Investigator Award<ref>{{cite web|title=Laura F. Landweber|url=https://www.sigmaxi.org/programs/prizes-awards/william-procter/award-winner/laura-f.-landweber|publisher=Sigma Xi|accessdate=27 November 2015}}</ref>

*2005 - [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Fellow<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/content/landweber-laura|title=AAAS Fellows|last=|first=|date=|website=AAAS|publisher=|access-date=12 November 2016|archive-date=November 13, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161113035051/https://www.aaas.org/content/landweber-laura|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*2008 - Regional Award Winner, [[Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists]], The New York Academy of Sciences<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blavatnikawards.org/honorees/profile/laura-landweber/|title=Laura Landweber|last=|first=|date=|website=Blavatnik Awards|publisher=|access-date=12 November 2016}}</ref>
*2012 - [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/laura-landweber/|title=Laura Landweber|last=|first=|date=|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|publisher=|access-date=12 November 2016}}</ref>
*2014 - Division R Lecturer, American Society for Microbiology<ref name=":0" />
*2017 - President, Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution<ref>[[Society for Molecular Biology and Evolution]]</ref>{{Circular reference|date=February 2025}}

== Personal life ==
Laura Landweber was married to physicist [[Steven Gubser]]<ref name="NYT20190906" /> and has three daughters.<ref name="NYT20190906" /><ref>{{cite magazine | first=Abigail | last=Jeffries | title=Ingenious, Innovative, and Interdisciplinary! | magazine=The New York Academy of Sciences Magazine | url=https://www.nyas.org/magazines/autumn-2008/ingenious-innovative-and-interdisciplinary/ | access-date=September 7, 2019 | pages=11–18 | issue=2, ''Autumn 2008'' | year=2008 | archive-date=September 22, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200922054312/https://www.nyas.org/magazines/autumn-2008/ingenious-innovative-and-interdisciplinary/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>
